# Independent audit: weighted three centroid tails and a contained endpoint



## Localization and closed central thresholds

For a full-dimensional convex body and nonzero direction, the scalar marginal is non-atomic. In dimension \(d\ge2\), its density has concave \((d-1)\)-st root, equivalently its probability law has the parameter \(1/d\le1/2\) required by the previously checked one-constraint Fradelizi–Guédon theorem. Dimension one is separately settled by the uniform interval identity.

The complement conversion to the weighted CDF objective is correct for these non-atomic laws. The zero-shift case follows directly from ordinary Grünbaum and \(\Gamma>1/3\), so localization is used only for \(s>0\).

If the centered CDF inequality is strictly violated, continuity at zero permits replacing only its central threshold by \(-\epsilon\), with \(0<\epsilon<s\), while preserving the violation. The resulting objective is affine and weakly upper semicontinuous on the fixed compact interval, because all three threshold sets are closed. Every admissible Dirac under \(\int x\,d\nu\ge0\) is at a nonnegative point and contributes to at most the \(+s\) term. Its objective is therefore at most one, strictly below \(2-\Gamma\). This explicitly includes the otherwise problematic Dirac at zero.

The non-Dirac localization alternative has mean exactly zero and density a nonnegative affine function to the power \(d-1\). For that law, the shifted objective is bounded above by the unshifted objective. Hence the scalar inequalities proved later apply without passing a Dirac limit through the central threshold. The mean constraint is the same single inequality used in the earlier audited localization theorem; no two-constraint reduction is assumed.

## Both affine-power orientations and every shift

For the increasing frustum law, the mean formula is exact. Pairing the increasing density around the interval midpoint gives \(m\ge(1+r)/2\). Concavity of the quantile gives \(p=G(m)\le1/2\); ordinary Grünbaum applied to the actual convex frustum gives \(p\ge\Gamma\).

The paired-tail theorem applies at shift \(1-m\), including the supporting endpoint at one, and gives exactly \(T_r=G(2m-1)\le1-2\Gamma\). This uses the already proved unweighted theorem, not the weighted theorem currently under audit.

In the increasing orientation, the weighted expression decreases up to \(s=1-m\) and then increases until constant. Its value at that point is \(1-p+(1-T_r)/2\), giving the stated lower bound.

In the reflected orientation, the expression is \(p+G(m-s)+G(m+s)/2\). Before the upper threshold reaches one, the derivative has the unique candidate zero

\[
              s_*=m\frac{1-k}{1+k},\qquad
              k=2^{-1/(d-1)},
\]

and changes from negative to positive if that zero lies in the interval. Both thresholds remain in support throughout \(0\le s\le1-m\), because \(2m-1\ge r\). After the upper threshold reaches one, the expression decreases to its constant value \(p+1/2\). Thus the two branches listed in Section 3 exhaust all global minima; neither support endpoint nor an intermediate shift is omitted.

At the interior candidate, \(k^{d-1}=1/2\) produces the coefficient \(A_d=[2/(1+k)]^{d-1}\) and the exact numerator \((1+A_d)m^d-(5/2)r^d\). The subsequent conversion to \(H(R)\) has the correct sign and denominator.

## Concavity closure and dimensional constant

I independently differentiated \(g(R)=I(R)^{1/\alpha}\), \(\alpha=1/d\). The second derivative is exactly

\[
 (1-\alpha)I^{1/\alpha-2}
 \left[\left(\int(1-t)a^{\alpha-1}\right)^2
      -\left(\int a^\alpha\right)
       \left(\int(1-t)^2a^{\alpha-2}\right)\right],
\]

which is nonpositive by Cauchy–Schwarz. Differentiation is justified on \(0<R<1\); continuity, rather than a nonexistent finite second derivative at zero, extends the concavity to the closed interval.

The mean is strictly increasing. Bernoulli's inequality gives the stated strict inequality between its initial value and \((1+k)/2\), so the unique critical endpoint \(R_*\) exists inside \((0,1)\). At this endpoint the critical upper threshold is exactly one. The endpoint value is \(p+G(2m-1)+1/2\ge\Gamma+1/2\), proving \(H(R_*)\ge0\). The other endpoint is \(A_d\Gamma-1/2\).

For \(d\ge3\), Jensen applied to \(x^{2/(d-1)}\) gives the power-mean bound \(A_d\ge8/(3+2\sqrt2)\). The strict rational comparison with \(15/11\) follows from \(43^2>30^2\cdot2\). The factorial-tail estimate gives \(e<1631/600<30/11\), and \((1+1/d)^d<e\) gives \(\Gamma>11/30\). Their product proves \(A_d\Gamma>1/2\). Dimension two is checked exactly by \(16/27>1/2\).

The function \(H\) is concave, so its two nonnegative endpoint values imply its nonnegativity throughout the critical interval. Constant affine densities are ordinary uniform interval laws and are handled directly. This closes both orientations in every stated dimension.

## Measurable subsets and actual three-fiber geometry

For any measurable \(A\subset K\), the lower bound \(|A\cap H_t|\ge\max\{0,a-V+F(t)\}\) is exact as a capacity statement. After subtracting \(a/2\), its minimum over \(0\le a\le V\) occurs at \(a=V-F(t)\). The value in equation (16) is correct, including the endpoint cases \(F(t)=0,V\).

For \(t\le0\), the new weighted theorem applies with \(s=-t\). For \(t\ge0\), the unweighted paired-tail theorem and monotonicity supply \((5/2)\Gamma V\ge(\Gamma+1/2)V\). Thus both signs of the arbitrary integer tilt are covered. Measurable subsets inherit the ambient hyperplane nullity, so no regularity of their boundaries is needed.

If \(A\) is convex, the prescribed three fibers at \(-1,0,1\) are the exact integer fibers of their convex hull: \((A+K)/2\subset K\) is the only required middle interpolation. Every nonvertical cap through \((0,g)\) has the opposite endpoint thresholds used in the inequality. Closed vertical caps retain the full middle fiber and have the stated masses. Other containing halfspaces contain their parallel through-point caps. The normalized depth comparison in (17) has the correct denominator \(2V+a\).

For translated large fibers, a shear in the continuous variables, depending affinely on the integer coordinate, makes them identical. The transformed midpoint inclusion then gives \(h_A+h_K\le2h_K\), forcing the transformed small endpoint inside \(K\). The lattice, halfspaces, and fiber volumes are preserved. The same middle ordinary centroid therefore has the asserted depth.

Each subset inequality charges its middle-fiber term. The final warning against summing many such pair inequalities while charging that middle term only once is necessary and correctly retained. No unrestricted mixed-integer conclusion follows from the stated special family alone.

## Common-core tolerance and the nested-chain consequence

For the common-core setting \(A\subset K\subset B\cap C\), the lower measure bound uses actual contained copies of \(K\), so it is valid for the original source. The mass denominator is \(2V+E+a\), where \(E=|B|+|C|-2V\). Solving the normalized comparison gives exactly \(E\le(1/\Gamma-1)a\), with no omitted factor of two. The vertical cap bounds continue to retain the full middle boundary fiber.

For a totally inclusion-ordered family in the stated convex-body setting, the middle member cannot lie below both endpoints unless all three coincide. Strict inclusion of full-dimensional compact convex bodies gives a strict volume increase, and Brunn–Minkowski would then make the endpoint midpoint body larger than the middle fiber. Thus an endpoint can be chosen as the smallest member.

With \(a\le V\le W\), the case \(W-V\ge a\) is precisely the condition that the largest fiber has at least half the total mass. Its own ordinary centroid supplies the desired mixed lower bound. In the remaining case \(E=W-V<a\), the common-core condition follows from \(\Gamma\le1/2\). Reversal and ties are handled correctly. This proves the nested-family conclusion in the stated positive-volume setting without reusing any source term or invoking OC itself.
